author: sonnet
label: c2-nat-sonnet-01
changes: Added a line to scope: the promotion tool, rollback command and evaluation job are CLI tools or a scheduled job, the only writers of the routing config, with each write recording its author (Q6).
Step 1 and step 8: stated that the poll runs on a background thread and a request never waits on it (Q1).
Step 3: stated that the model reads only its required features by name, runs in-process, and defined scored items (Q2, Q3).
Step 4: stated the popular list is one global list for all users (Q4).
Step 5: added request time to the message and said the sender is a thread in the API process (Q5, Q8).
Step 6: said the feature union is rebuilt from the routing config each run, so old previous features drop at the next run after promotion (Q7).
Step 9 and 11: defined the 7-day clock as continuous, reset by any restart (Q9). Open item 3 reworded to match.
Step 10: defined feature age as request time minus materialized_at, and said the workers are a separate service consuming the queue (Q5, Q8).
Step 11: reports now carry a report ID and each run adds a new one (Q10).

Step 12: approval is now tied to the version and a report no older than 24 hours, and the latest report must also pass the numbers. Replaced the exact-report rule that could never survive hourly reports (Q10).
Added open item 8 listing the unspecified platform choices: inference runtime, queue product, worker deployment, popularity scoring, filter rules (Q2, Q4, Q5).
Step 1: defined ready (config read, active and previous models loaded) to answer Q13.
Step 3: added a line on where candidate item IDs come from (undefined, open item) and that the API checks the deadline around inference, for Q11 and Q12.
Step 5: added shadow volume and batched sending, and replaced the automatic disable on high drop rate with an alert plus the manual kill switch, since nothing was defined to perform it (Q14).
Routing config note and steps 9 to 11: a new salt per shadow start serves as run ID; results carry shadow_salt and the evaluation job counts only the current run (Q16).
Step 10: the worker discards messages when shadow is null in the current config (Q15).
Step 11: noted that reports stay attached to the version after promotion (Q15).
Step 8: load runs in the background while requests use the current model, and only active and previous stay resident (Q17).
Open item 8: added model artifact format, candidate source and request rate to the unspecified list.
Step 3: if fewer than 20 items remain after filtering, top up from the popular list; empty result counts as inference failure (Q18).
Step 4: defined reason timeout as the feature lookup only, inference error and missed inference deadline as inference_error, and noted the fallback fits in 150 ms (Q23).
Step 5: stated that the API does not check candidate features and the worker records the skip (Q24).

Routing config note, step 6 and step 9: fixed a real gap by making shadow start in two phases (percent 0 prepare, then percent 10 start), so the materialization job includes the candidate's features before any user is sent to it, with no separate job config (Q22).
Assumptions and step 10: defined the kill switch as the promotion tool's stop-shadow command, run by the ML engineer or the on-call engineer (Q20).
Steps 8 and 14: stated that instances do not preload the candidate, load after the promotion write, and keep the old active meanwhile (Q19).
Step 14: defined how promotion completion is measured from instance health metrics, with a 5 minute wait and a human decision for stragglers (Q21).
Open item 8: added where instance health metrics are kept.
Step 1: added that the API never loads or runs the candidate and needs only percent and salt (Q25).
Step 9: defined one feature check (sampled records, per-feature share, blocks only if a feature is absent from the whole sample) used in both phases and step 12 (Q26, Q27).
Step 9 and step 11: the 7-day clock now starts at the recorded write time of the percent-10 start, instead of the first result, so the evaluation job can read it (Q30).
Step 12: promotion feature re-check now refers to the step 9 feature check (Q26).
Step 6 and step 14: added that the union covers the promotion window so materialization is safe during the switch (Q28, Q29).
Step 10: added how workers learn of and load the candidate (Q31).
Open items: reworded item 3 for the new clock, added item 8 for sample size, renumbered platform choices to item 9.
Step 14: rollback now swaps active and previous (previous holds the version rolled back from), so both stay resident and in the materialization union, and the command can roll forward.

Step 10: candidate inference uses the same 125 ms deadline as the active model. A miss is a candidate error, a result between 80 ms and 125 ms only counts in p99 latency, and a timed-out attempt is recorded as 125 ms.
Step 4: the popular list is refreshed by each instance on a background thread every 10 minutes (proposal) from the daily table or object, with the last good list kept on failure.
Open items: added item 10 for the popular list refresh interval.
Reordered into summary, terms, fixed rules and assumptions, state table, then steps, then a failure table, then open questions.
Split the 14 steps into 'How the system runs' (steps 1-8) and 'How a model is tested and released' (steps 9-14).
Rewrote the summary to describe the nightly-table system today and the main flow in three sentences.

Added a terms section defining the online feature store, materialization, model registry, routing config, active/previous/candidate, shadow, shadow worker, fallback, gate report and the command-line tools.
Folded the writer assumptions and the kill switch definition into the terms (the kill switch is the stop-shadow command, not a fourth writer).
Moved the brief's fixed numbers (150 ms, 30 ms, 6 hours, 1 minute, 10%, 7 days, 0.5%, 80 ms, ML lead approval) into one fixed-rules list and kept the budget table.
Put every step into the same four-part form: trigger, what it does, data kept, if it goes wrong.
Removed the repeated statements of the feature check, the union rule, the 125 ms deadline and the 24-hour approval rule, so each is said once.
Merged the repeated rollback and previous-resident explanations into step 14.
Merged the two separate explanations of the 7-day clock into steps 9 and 11.
Dropped the duplicated notes on instance disagreement and load time. Kept one line each in steps 8 and 14.
Replaced references to open-item numbers and step-number codes with descriptive wording in most places.
Added a failure summary table.
Merged open items 8 and 9 details (queue, runtime, filters, catalogue source, request rate) into one platform-choices item and added the tool authentication method to it.
Added to step 3 a statement that the API runs the model in-process, and to the assumptions the fact that shadow output is read by nothing on the request path.
Cut: the line that the API takes a pointer 'for the rest of this request' is kept; the explanation of why dropped messages differ from errors was shortened.

Nothing was removed from the first version's requirements, limits or numbers. Checked line by line, including the 20-item response, 2-missed-run and 4-hour alerts, 24-hour report age, overlap@20 metrics and the A/B option details.
holes: Q2: What does 'inference' actually run on in the API process (CPU, GPU, a library, a separate model server)? And what exactly are 'scored items' before 'removes duplicates and filters'? (author: The brief does not name the runtime. I assumed the model runs in-process in the API (step 10 says shadow uses the same inference code). Scored items are candidate item IDs with a model score, best first. The exact filter rules are not defined; added to open items.)

Q4: What is the 'popular list' and how is it computed in the daily job? Is it the same for every user? (author: The brief says only that a popular-items list is recomputed daily. It is one global list, the same for every user. How popularity is scored is not specified; added to open items.)

Q5: In step 5, what does the 'background sender' run as, and what is the 'message queue' (which product, who consumes it)? How do shadow workers get deployed and who runs them? (author: The sender is a background thread in the API process. The queue product, who deploys the shadow workers and who runs them are not specified in the brief; added to open items. Workers are a separate service that consumes the queue.)

Q11: Step 3 says inference is in-process, but what exactly is the 'model' object loaded from the registry (a file format, a library)? Does the API process need to understand it, and how does it run one request's scoring with the 125 ms deadline enforced? (author: The brief names no artifact format or inference runtime, so I cannot say what the model object is. I added a line to step 3 that the API checks remaining time before and after inference and treats a missed deadline as a failure, and listed format and runtime under open item 8.)

Q12: Where do the 'candidate item IDs' come from that the model scores? Does the model score the whole catalogue, or is there an earlier retrieval step the document does not show? (author: The brief does not say whether the model scores the whole catalogue or sits behind a retrieval step. I treat it as part of what the model artifact does. Added a line in step 3 and to open item 8.)

Q14: In step 5, the message carries the whole feature record and 20 items. How many requests per second are in shadow, and how does a message reach the queue from the background sender (batching, one by one)? What does 'disabled automatically if the drop rate stays high' do, and who writes that change? (author: The brief gives no request rate. Shadow volume is 10% of non-fallback requests; I added that to step 5 and listed the rate as an open item. The sender ships in small batches. I removed the automatic disable on high drop rate, since nothing was defined to write that change. A high drop rate now raises an alert and the on-call uses the kill switch.)

Q17: Step 8 says an instance loads a version it does not hold when active or previous changes. How long does a load take and how does it keep serving while loading? Also when does an instance drop an old version from memory? (author: Real load time is not known; it stays open item 5. Loading runs on the instance's background thread while requests keep using the current model, and the pointer swaps only after the load succeeds. An instance keeps exactly active and previous, and drops other versions once no in-flight request holds them. Added to step 8.)
